title: Materializing split, mixed, and three-body interactions using rotor-based mechanical hysterons
authors: Oche T. Ali, Faten A. Al Ardat, Jack Feider, Harry Maakestad, Alex Walk, Zachariah S. Schrecengost, Joseph D. Paulsen
abstract: Interacting hysteretic spins are an appealing model for cyclically-driven athermal disordered matter. Because they provide a basis for storing and processing information from their environment, such models are also being pursued as a framework for intelligent matter. Recent proof-of-concept designs have begun to demonstrate the strong, controlled, pairwise interactions that are necessary for this endeavor. But, it is not yet clear what are the limits---practically or fundamentally---on such interactions. Here we build rotor-based mechanical hysterons that extend the generality of their interactions in three ways: (i) splitting the interaction strength based on the hysteron state, (ii) building a non-reciprocal interaction of mixed sign, and (iii) incorporating tunable three-body effects. We access these effects within a simple, replicable design platform, and we rationalize our results. Our work expands the space of behaviors for designed structures that compute on mechanical inputs.
summary: The paper details the construction of rotor-based mechanical hysterons capable of realizing highly controllable and complex interactions. By manipulating geometric parameters like spring mounting positions and rotor angles, the authors achieve tunable split, mixed-sign, and three-body coupling terms in a physical system. This work expands the design space for mechanically computing matter based on interacting disordered elements.
main_problem: To systematically demonstrate control over complex interaction types—split, mixed, and three-body interactions—in a mechanical system designed to model hysteretic spins.
main_result: The authors successfully build rotor-based mechanical hysterons that exhibit tunable non-reciprocal, state-dependent pairwise couplings and controllable three-body effects by manipulating geometric parameters.
method: The study combines analytical derivations based on torque balance equations with experimental realization using coupled rotors to map abstract interaction terms onto physical hardware.
model_or_system: The system consists of rotor hysterons coupled by mechanical springs, modeling interacting spins relevant for studying athermal disordered matter and developing intelligent matter.
key_observables: Switching thresholds (gamma), pairwise interaction strengths ($J_{\pm}^{ij}$), and three-body coupling terms ($K^{\pm}_{ijk}$).
important_parameters: Spring stiffnesses ($k$), rotor angles ($	heta$), mounting positions ($\ell$), and the ratio of spring rest lengths to separation distances ($x_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations derived from small coupling spring rest lengths, though the work explicitly explores regimes where these assumptions break down.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the splitting of interaction strengths by varying rotor angles or mounting positions, demonstrate pseudoavalanches requiring mixed interactions, and show the emergence of three-body terms when nonlinear torque regimes are accessed.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general hysteretic model and its required interactions to demonstrating symmetry breaking (splitting), then showing how mixed signs can be engineered, culminating in the realization of tunable three-body effects.
why_interesting: This work provides a tangible, mechanical platform for studying concepts typically confined to abstract spin models or theoretical Hamiltonians, offering experimental insight into non-equilibrium dynamics and complex many-body interactions relevant to disordered systems.

FIG. 4. Geometric origin of mixed interactions. (a) Contour plot of Eq. 2 for the torque τ12 on rotor 1 due to a single coupling spring of rest length x0. One end of the spring is mounted at ℓ1 on rotor 1 and the other is held at an arbitrary location. (b) We may approximate x0 ≃0 for springs mounted to a second rotor a distance w ≫x0 away. Cyan arrows: Typical case where increasing θ2 increases the torque on rotor 1 for uncrossed springs and decreases the torque on rotor 2 for crossed springs. Yellow arrows: When the angle between the rotors exceeds 90◦, this relationship inverts. Mixed interactions are built by inverting this relationship for some of the states.
